1:
The chapter opens on a phrase that at once raises a question of time. The reformed John Gill insists that 'on that day' cannot mean the day the wall was dedicated, nor soon after, for a people could not be so corrupted so quickly; it points rather to the season when Nehemiah, having governed twelve years and gone back to Babylon, had returned again to Jerusalem. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses agree. Adam Clarke, following Calmet, holds that the transactions of this chapter did not immediately succeed the dedication: Nehemiah returned to the Persian court in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, and after about a year obtained leave to revisit Judah, where he found the evils here recorded. John Wesley likewise takes 'that day' loosely, as a certain day after a long absence in which errors and abuses had crept in.

On the substance the witnesses gather around the public reading of the law. On that day the book was read in the people's hearing, and in it was found the statute that the Ammonite and Moabite should not come into the congregation of God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the reading itself the lesson: it was Israel's honour and the great preservation of their holiness that they were a peculiar people, not to mingle with the nations; and here is the benefit of the public reading of the word, that when duly attended to it discovers sin and duty, good and evil, and shows us wherein we have erred. Then we profit by the discovery, he says, when we are wrought upon to separate ourselves from the evil to which we had addicted ourselves — as the people here put away the mixed multitude that had of old been a snare, the multitude that fell a lusting in Num. 11:4. The statute and its reason, Henry notes, stand together in Deut. 23:3-5.

Beneath the agreement lies a real difference over what the law forbade. Clarke reads it narrowly: 'ye shall not form any kind of matrimonial alliance with them,' and adds emphatically, 'this, and this alone, is the meaning of the law.' Wesley reads it more broadly — not to be incorporated into the commonwealth of Israel, nor joined with any Israelite in marriage — and Henry broadest of all, that the Ammonites and Moabites should not be naturalized, should not settle among them nor unite with them, these inmates being expelled as usurpers and dangerous. So the schools divide over the reach of the exclusion, whether it bars only intermarriage or bars naturalization and settlement as well. What none of them doubts is the ground the text gives for it, drawn out in the next verse: an ancient enmity that God had neither forgotten nor excused.
2:
The reason annexed to the law occupies the witnesses, for it explains why a grudge of a thousand years still stood in force. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the ground the verse names: the Ammonites and Moabites met not the children of Israel with bread and with water, but hired Balaam against them that he should curse them — 'howbeit our God turned the curse into a blessing.' The two nations had refused the common courtesies of the road to a people who had done them no harm, and had gone further and paid a prophet to imprecate ruin upon them; the memory of that hostility, and of God's reversal of it, is what the reading revived.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the aggravation. The reason given, he says, is that these nations had been injurious and ill-natured to the Israel of God — they had not shown them so much as common civility, but sought their ruin, though Israel not only did them no harm but were expressly forbidden to do them any. The offence, in other words, was unprovoked malice repaid for restraint; and it was fitting that a people who would not meet Israel with bread should not themselves be received into the congregation. The reformed John Gill sends the reader to the fuller account of the same story, where the hiring of Balaam and the turning of the curse are set down at large, treating this verse as the compressed echo of that history.

Keil and Delitzsch add a word on the date and on the crowd that was purged. The precise time of the occurrence cannot be fixed from the phrase 'on that day,' since public readings of the law were frequent in those days, as the seventh-month assemblies of the earlier chapters show, when the book was read not on one day only but daily through the feast. And they observe that the miracle named here — the curse turned to blessing — is the standing proof that the enmity of Ammon and Moab could not finally prevail, for the God who overruled Balaam's mouth was the same God now separating his people from every heathen alliance. The witnesses do not divide. Together they let the verse do its work: it is not spite but righteousness that bars the door, the settled recompense of nations who met grace with a hired curse, and whose malice God had already, once for all, bent back into good for the people they meant to destroy. The reading of the ancient reason becomes, in Nehemiah's hand, the warrant for a present reform.
3:
When the law had been heard and understood, the people acted upon it at once, and the witnesses fasten on both the promptness of the obedience and the identity of those put away. The reformed John Gill takes the law heard to be that concerning the Ammonite and Moabite, which by extension reached other nations and forbade marriage with them; the hearing bred immediate compliance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the term rendered 'mixed multitude': it is the word used in Exod. 12:38 of the non-Israelitish crowd that followed Israel out of Egypt, here transferred to the strangers of different heathen nationalities living among the people, all of whom were separated from Israel once the law was rightly weighed.

Over exactly who was separated the schools diverge a little. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the purge widely on one axis and narrowly on another: they excluded all strange women, and all persons, young and old, who had been born of these illegal connections — that is, the foreign wives and the mixed children together. John Wesley takes the 'multitude' as all the heathenish people with whom they had contracted alliance, casting the net over the whole body of intermarried and confederate foreigners. Keil and Delitzsch, keeping to the philology, hold it to be simply the resident strangers of assorted nations dwelling among the Jews. The difference is one of emphasis — whether the text pictures chiefly the foreign wives and their offspring, or the heathen allies as a class, or the mixed population at large — but all agree that the separation was thorough and immediate.

The deeper note the witnesses share is the power of the word to move a people. Gill and the others let the sequence stand as its own lesson: the law was read, the law was understood, and the law was obeyed, without the long delay that so often follows conviction. It is the same benefit the puritan tradition found in the reading itself — that Scripture, duly attended to, not only discovers sin but works the will to part from it. Here the discovery of the old statute against Ammon and Moab did not lie idle in the ear; it passed at once into act, and the mixed multitude that had of old been Israel's snare was put out. The witnesses do not contend over the fact, only over its precise scope; and they leave the verse as a model of hearing that does not stop at hearing, a congregation that, finding itself in fault, made haste to mend rather than to excuse. What the law prescribed on the page, the people performed in the street the same day.
4:
The narrative now turns back to the root of the disorder, and the witnesses meet a difficulty of identity at the threshold. The verse names Eliashib the priest, having the oversight of the chamber of the house of God, as allied unto Tobiah — and the first question is whether this Eliashib is the high priest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch judge that he is, the same high priest named in the earlier chapters, inferring it from the very fact that he was 'set over the chambers of the house of our God,' a control his office alone would confer. Charles Ellicott agrees that he is probably the high priest of Nehemiah 3:1, and notices tellingly the suspicious absence of Eliashib's name throughout the high religious festivities of the preceding chapters, as though he had held aloof from them. John Wesley states it flatly: Eliashib the high priest, having the chief power over the house of God and all its chambers.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enters the one note of doubt. Perhaps, he says, this was a different person from Eliashib the high priest; yet there is no indubitable evidence that he was not the same — and if he was, he was grievously unfaithful to his high charge and a reproach to the priesthood. Clarke traces the alliance for us: Eliashib had married his grandson to Sanballat's daughter, which produced a connection with Tobiah, the fast friend of Sanballat, and in Tobiah's favour he polluted the house of God. The reformed John Gill simply marks the timing — this was 'before' the law had been read and acted upon — setting the corruption in its place before the reform.

How the alliance stood the witnesses cannot fully say, and Ellicott is candid that the manner of it 'is not stated.' What they can say is heavy enough. Tobiah the Ammonite — the very sort of man the law just read had shut out of the congregation — had been drawn by marriage and friendship into the innermost circle of the priesthood, and the chief priest himself had become his patron. The chamber over which Eliashib presided was no private closet but part of the series of store-rooms running round the temple, the appointed reception of the tithes and oblations that came to the house of God. That such a place, and such a keeper, should be turned to the service of an Ammonite enemy is the scandal the following verses expose. The witnesses converge on its gravity: whether Eliashib was high priest or only a priest of rank, the guardian of the sanctuary's stores had opened them to the sanctuary's foe.
5:
The extent of Eliashib's favour is measured by the room he made, and the witnesses reckon both its construction and its cost. The reformed John Gill notes that the chamber was 'great' because several smaller ones had been thrown into a single apartment, the partitions taken down, as Piscator observed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms it from the sequel — many small chambers had been united into one — and Keil and Delitzsch spell out what that one great chamber had formerly held: the meat offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of corn, new wine, and oil that were commanded to be given to the Levites, the singers, and the porters, together with the offerings of the priests. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the purpose of the alteration: by removing the sacred things and uniting the small chambers, Eliashib furnished a lodging for Tobiah when he came to Jerusalem, that he might have the freer communication with him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry pours out his indignation at what this meant. It was a wretched thing, he says, on four counts at once: that Tobiah the Ammonite should be entertained with respect and given a magnificent reception in Israel; that the high priest, who should have taught the people the law and set them an example, should against the law give him entertainment, abusing the very power he held as overseer of the chambers; that he should lodge him in the courts of God's house, as if to confront God himself — an act, Henry says, next to setting up an idol there, as the wicked kings of old had done, when an Ammonite ought not so much as to come into the congregation; and that he should throw out the temple's stores to make room for him, exposing them to be lost, wasted, and embezzled, though they were the portions of the priests. Thus, Henry adds, did Eliashib corrupt the covenant of Levi that Malachi complained of at this very time in Mal. 2:8.

The witnesses do not divide; together they render the offence in its full colour. The chamber that had been a treasury of holy things — the maintenance of the ministers, the substance of the worship — was emptied of its sacred contents and fitted up as a guest-room for the man who had laboured hardest to stop the walls from rising. Gill and Ellicott fix the physical alteration, Keil and Delitzsch the holy uses displaced, Wesley the intimacy sought, and Henry the accumulated scandal of it; and all agree that the desecration was the more monstrous for the hand that wrought it. The priest who should have guarded the stores had spent them on the enemy, and made the house of God a lodging for an Ammonite.
6:
A single parenthesis explains how such a thing could happen, and the witnesses seize on it as the hinge of the whole account. 'But in all this time was not I at Jerusalem.' The reformed John Gill draws the plain inference: Nehemiah was absent all the while these things were done by Eliashib, or otherwise they would never have been suffered. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the absence into a proverb of vigilance — the envious one who sows tares in God's field knows how to take his opportunity when the servants sleep or are away, as in Matt. 13:25; the golden calf was made while Moses was up in the mount, as at Exod. 32:1. Had Nehemiah been present, he says, the high priest durst not have done such a thing.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the chronology in order. Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes and remained twelve years, till the thirty-second; then he returned to Babylon and stayed about a year; then, obtaining leave, he came again to revisit his brethren, and found matters as this chapter describes. John Wesley reads the verse the same way — Eliashib took the occasion of Nehemiah's absence to do these things — noting that the governor had gone from Jerusalem, where he had been present once and again.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over two details of the wording. The verse is a parenthetical explanation of the disorderly state of things, inserted to account for how the corruption grew unchecked. And Nehemiah calls Artaxerxes 'king of Babylon,' not king of Persia, probably, Ellicott suggests, because it was at Babylon that he found the court and rejoined the king. The phrase 'after certain days' leaves the interval indefinite, but the mention of the thirty-second year shows that he had been twelve years in Jerusalem before his return to the royal presence. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the whole tangle of Tobiah in the temple and the Levites in their fields grew up precisely because the one man zealous for the house of God was far away at court; and they agree that his coming back is about to reverse it all. The verse is thus both an excuse offered for the community and a warning left for every age — that good order kept by one strong hand may unravel the moment that hand is withdrawn, and that the enemy watches for exactly such an hour.
7:
Nehemiah's return and his discovery are told in a breath, and the witnesses attend to the force of the words. The reformed John Gill notes that he came to Jerusalem through the king's leave and with a commission from him, so that he arrived clothed again with authority to act. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix his first concern: on his return he directed his attention to the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a chamber in the courts of the house of God. The verb rendered 'understood' or 'perceived,' they observe, is the same used elsewhere of coming to a clear and considered knowledge of a matter — Nehemiah did not act on rumour but grasped exactly what had been done and by whom.

The witnesses read the moment against the parenthesis just before it. The corruption had grown in his absence; now the absence is over, and the man who had built the walls turns his eye upon the far graver breach within them. The puritan-evangelical tradition, following Matthew Henry's account of the whole episode, marks how it grieved a good governor to the heart to learn what intimacy had sprung up between the chief priest and the chief enemy — that God's house should be so profaned, his adversaries so caressed and trusted, and his cause betrayed by the very man who should have been its protector and patron. Nothing grieves a good magistrate more, Henry says, than to see the ministers of God's house do a wicked thing.

Keil and Delitzsch stress the exact charge the verse lays. The evil is named twice over — 'the evil that Eliashib did for Tobiah' — so that the blame is fastened not on Tobiah the intruder, who did but take what was offered, but on Eliashib the host, who as guardian of the sacred stores had prepared the intrusion. The scene of it, too, is emphasized: not merely a chamber, but 'a chamber in the courts of the house of God,' the profanation reaching into the very precincts consecrated to worship. The witnesses do not divide. They let the verse stand as the moment of reckoning — the return of the reformer, the clear-eyed grasp of the wrong, and the identifying of the true offender — poised on the edge of the vigorous action the next verse records. Nehemiah has power again, Henry adds, and he will use it for God; the perceiving of the evil in this verse is the drawn breath before the blow that expels it.
8:
The reformer's grief passes at once into action, and the witnesses feel the heat of it. 'It grieved me sore: therefore I cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the chamber.' The reformed John Gill fixes the ground of the grief — that so sacred a place should be turned to common use, and to the use of a heathen, and of an enemy to the Jews and their religion. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the whole sweep of the act: so greatly was Nehemiah displeased that he flung out all Tobiah's furniture, commanded the chamber to be purified, and had the vessels of the house of God, the meat offering and the frankincense, and probably the tithes and heave offerings too, brought back into it. From the very phrase 'household stuff,' they add, it appears that Tobiah had been using the chamber as a dwelling whenever he came from time to time to Jerusalem — it was no mere store-room lent, but a residence established for the enemy in the temple.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts the deed to its great precedent. Nehemiah acted, he says, as Jesus Christ acted when he found the courts of the Lord's house profaned, overthrowing the tables of the money-changers and the seats of them that sold doves, as at Matt. 21:12. The zeal is the same zeal for the purity of God's house, and the summary violence of it — the goods hurled out into the open — is of a piece with the cleansing of the temple. John Wesley adds the aggravations that justified the heat: the place was polluted by one who in many respects ought never to have come there, being no priest, a stranger, an Ammonite, and one of the worst of that people, and all of it done by the permission and order of the high priest himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the emotion for the second time in the chapter. Nehemiah's deep feeling here springs, he says, from two things at once: the utter dissoluteness of which this abuse was a token, and the fact that it was a priestly desecration, the sin of the man set to guard the sanctuary. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the profanation, Keil and Delitzsch the sweep of the restoration, Clarke the Christlike zeal, Wesley the enormity of host and guest alike, and Ellicott the double wound to a godly heart. Together they show a governor who would not temporize with a settled evil, but emptied the chamber of the enemy with his own hand — and, having cast out the intruder's goods, made ready to bring the holy things home.
9:
The casting-out is completed by a cleansing, and the witnesses note the care with which the holy place was reclaimed. The reformed John Gill observes that the plural, 'they cleansed the chambers,' shows there had been more than one room, or several thrown into one; and that the purifying was not by washing only, for the pollution was ceremonial, contracted by the habitation of a heathen in them. He supposes it was done by the water of separation, the appointed remedy for such uncleanness prescribed in Num. 19:9. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch complete the movement: when the chambers were cleansed, Nehemiah brought again into them the vessels of the house of God, with the meat offering and the frankincense, restoring the store-rooms to the sacred use from which Eliashib had diverted them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a fine observation on the order of events. There was, he says, a formal purification of the chambers; and it is a note of minute accuracy in the narrative that no mention is yet made of the tithes being brought back — only the vessels, the meat offering, and the frankincense. The tithes are held over, for the next verses will show why: the Levites who should have received them had been driven from their posts, and the machinery of the tithe had broken down. The historian records exactly what could be restored at once, and defers what could not, a precision Ellicott takes as a mark of the account's truthfulness.

The witnesses do not divide, and the puritan tradition finds in the sequence a parable of the soul. As Matthew Henry read the whole episode, the casting-out of Tobiah's stuff and the cleansing of the chamber before the vessels return is a picture of repentance and renewal: those who would expel sin from the heart, the living temple, must first throw out its household stuff and all the provision made for it, and then, when sin is cast out, let the blood of Christ be applied by faith and the room be furnished afresh with the graces of God's Spirit for every good work. Whether taken as history or as figure, the verse marks a completed reversal. The intruder's goods are gone, the defiled rooms are ritually purged, and the sacred vessels stand again in their places. Gill fixes the mode of the cleansing, Keil and Delitzsch the restoration of the holy things, and Ellicott the careful withholding of the tithes; together they leave the temple's stores half-recovered, awaiting the further reform that the plight of the Levites will require.
10:
The half-finished restoration exposes a deeper wound, and the witnesses trace it to its cause. Nehemiah perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them, so that the Levites and the singers who did the work were fled every one to his field. The reformed John Gill weighs how it came about: the tithes, once removed to make room for Tobiah, might have been converted to other uses; or the people, seeing what Eliashib had done, ceased to bring them in, judging they would be misapplied; and the Levites, unpaid, had simply deserted their station. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the mechanism plainly — the Levites, singers, and porters used to receive their daily portions of the tithes and first-fruits during their ministry; when those offerings were discontinued, they were forced to seek their maintenance from the fields of the towns where they dwelt, and so forsook the service of the house of God. Charles Ellicott points to the same fields, the lands apportioned to them in the Levitical cities under Numbers 35:2.

Over the precise cause the witnesses spread a little. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lays out the alternatives: the portions were withheld either by the corrupt high priest Eliashib, who took them to his own use or spent them entertaining Tobiah and his great allies, or by the people, who out of covetousness kept back their tithes contrary to their own solemn agreement, or who so abhorred Eliashib's abuse of sacred things that they neglected to bring in dues they knew would be perverted. Adam Clarke lays the blame squarely on the rulers who permitted all these abuses. So the schools differ over whether priest or people or magistrate most failed — though all agree the Levites were the sufferers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lasting lesson. If ministers have not the encouragement they should, he says, let them consider whether they be not themselves accessory to the contempt they are under, by neglecting their business — for the Levite in his field, the clergyman keeping the market, is out of his place; God's house is his place, and there let him be found. Yet he adds the sharper edge: a scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry; the work is neglected because the workmen are, and men who would not starve their own servants had starved out the servants of God. Henry marvels how quickly it decayed, for the payment of the singers had lately been put into good method, and yet already failed for want of being looked after. The witnesses converge: the tithe that fed the worship had dried up, the ministers had scattered to survive, and the house of God stood forsaken for want of bread.
11:
The governor's response is confrontation, and the witnesses attend to whom he confronted and with what words. 'Then contended I with the rulers, and said, Why is the house of God forsaken?' The reformed John Gill takes the rulers to be the ecclesiastical officers, the priests appointed over the chambers, whom Nehemiah expostulated with warmly and chid severely for their conduct. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify them rather as the seganim, the heads of the community, whose duty it was to see that the tithes were regularly brought to the house of God; hence Nehemiah's rebuke, 'Why is the house of God forsaken?' — forsaken through the non-delivery of its dues. Charles Ellicott names the offence beneath the neglect: the rich men had taken advantage of Nehemiah's absence to indulge their covetousness, breaking the express covenant they had sworn.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the reproach with the very words of that covenant. The people had solemnly promised in Nehemiah 10:39 that they would never forsake the house of their God; and here, Clarke notes, Nehemiah used their own words back to them by way of reproof — 'Why is the house of God forsaken?' echoes 'we will not forsake the house of our God.' John Wesley reads the rebuke as aimed at the priests to whom the management of these things was committed, charged both with neglect of duty and with breach of their late solemn promise: 'you have not only injured men in withholding their dues, but you have occasioned the neglect of God's house and service.'

All the witnesses agree on the remedy that followed the rebuke. Nehemiah gathered the Levites together and set them in their place — brought them back, Keil and Delitzsch say, from their several country possessions to Jerusalem and to the performance of their official duties. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays the fault upon the rulers as Nehemiah did, for it is required of Christian magistrates that they use their power to oblige ministers to do their duty and people to do theirs; both ministers and people who forsake religion, and magistrates who do not keep them to it, will have much to answer for. And he adds the encouraging note that many who are careless would do far better if they were but called upon — many that neglected their posts returned to them the moment a resolute governor demanded it. The witnesses do not finally divide over who the 'rulers' were, whether priests or civic heads or the covetous rich; they agree that Nehemiah found the sanctuary abandoned, named the shame of it, and by one firm act of authority set the ministers back in their stations.
12:
The rebuke bears fruit at once, and the witnesses mark the swift turn from neglect to obedience. 'Then brought all Judah the tithe of the corn and the new wine and the oil unto the treasuries.' The reformed John Gill reads the change of heart behind it: when the people saw a reformation made, and things going in their proper channel, and a right use likely to be made of their tithes — these now given to the proper persons, reinstated in their office — they brought their dues again. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reasons the same way: they brought them out of the respect they bore to Nehemiah, and because they saw the tithes would now be applied to their proper uses, no longer diverted to a Tobiah or embezzled by a faithless priest.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the sequence of the reform. The Levites once restored to their place, all Judah — the whole community — brought the tithe of corn, wine, and oil into the store-chambers of the temple, and Nehemiah proceeded to organize the receipt and distribution of what was brought. They connect it to the earlier covenant obligation the people had taken upon themselves, so that the renewed giving is not a novelty but a return to a pledge lately made and lately broken.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the principle the verse teaches. Nehemiah's zeal provoked theirs, he says; when the people saw the Levites at their work again, they could not for shame withhold their wages any longer, but honestly and cheerfully brought them in. And he lays down the rule of it: the better church-work is done, the better will church-dues be paid — restore the ministry to its diligence, and the people's liberality revives to support it. The two failures had fed each other, the Levites scattering because unpaid and the people withholding because the Levites were scattered; and now the two recoveries feed each other, the ministers returning to their posts and the people returning to their tithes. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley fix the confidence that unlocked the people's hand, Keil and Delitzsch the ordered channel into which the tithe now flowed, and Henry the reciprocal quickening of duty on both sides. Together they show how quickly a single act of resolute reform could reverse a settled decay: the house of God, forsaken a verse before, is filled again with the corn and wine and oil of a people whose willingness had only waited upon an honest administration to trust.
13:
The inflow of tithes required trustworthy hands, and the witnesses dwell on the men Nehemiah chose. 'And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah; and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur.' The reformed John Gill notes that these were new treasurers, appointed because the former officers were either dead or unfaithful to their trust. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks the criterion and the caution: they were chosen faithful by the consent of those who knew them, and Nehemiah now sought such men the more diligently because he had had experience of the perfidiousness of the former trustees. Adam Clarke fills out the phrase 'they were counted faithful' — they were reported to him as persons in whom he could confide, men who had been steady in God's ways and work while others had grown careless and relaxed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sees in the appointment the genius of the reform. The whole was made effectual by organization: Eliashib had failed in his duty, and the appointment of treasurers is now confirmed and secured. He notes the balanced composition of the board — a priest, a scribe, a Levite, and, as under-steward, a layman named Hanan — men mentioned in connection with the building of the wall, and all of them faithful; since the majority were priests and Levites, their office was fittingly to distribute to their brethren the priests and Levites. Ellicott even suggests that Zadok the scribe was the secretary of Nehemiah, the same named among the sealers of the covenant.

The witnesses converge on the wisdom of the arrangement, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies its rule. These commissioners were such as were accounted faithful, that is, had approved themselves so in other trusts committed to them, and so had purchased to themselves a good degree, in the manner of 1 Timothy 3:13. Let men be tried first and then trusted, Henry says, tried in the less and then trusted with more; their office was to receive and to pay, to distribute to their brethren in due season and due proportion. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley fix the reason for a new board, Clarke and Ellicott the character and balance of its members, and Henry the principle that stewardship of holy things must be committed only to proven fidelity. Together they show Nehemiah building not merely a burst of obedience but a lasting structure, so that the tithe restored in the last verse should not fail again for want of honest men to keep it.
14:
His work for the house of God finished for the moment, Nehemiah turns to prayer, and the witnesses weigh the temper of it. 'Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and wipe not out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God, and for the offices thereof.' The reformed John Gill guards the request from any taint of desert: Nehemiah asks to be remembered not in a way of strict justice, as if he had merited anything at God's hand, but in a way of grace and mercy, that God would graciously accept what was done for the honour of his name and overlook all the failings and infirmities in it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the petition at its plain worth — the transaction just related gave Nehemiah occasion to commit his labour for the sanctuary and its offices to the merciful remembrance of God — and Charles Ellicott hears in it once more the faithful servant begging a merciful remembrance of what he had done for the honour of God in the observances of his temple.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the second clause as its own confession. 'Wipe not out my good deeds' means, Clarke says, that if God were strict to mark what is done amiss, even the good deeds must be wiped out; therefore Nehemiah casts himself on mercy — 'Lord, remember me in thy mercy, and let my upright conduct be acceptable to thee.' The prayer thus disowns merit in the very act of pleading service, seeking not a wage earned but a work graciously owned.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the modesty and the confidence together. Nehemiah refers it to God to consider him, not in pride as boasting, nor as though he had made God a debtor, but in a humble appeal to his integrity and honest intention, and in the believing expectation that God will not be unrighteous to forget his work and labour of love, according to Hebrews 6:10. Observe, Henry adds, how modest his request is — he prays 'Remember me,' not 'Reward me'; 'wipe not out my good deeds,' not 'publish them' or 'record them'; yet he was rewarded and his deeds were recorded, for God does more than we are able to ask. Deeds done for the house of God and the support of religion are good deeds, in which there is both righteousness and godliness, and God will surely remember them. The witnesses do not divide. They leave Nehemiah where he leaves himself — not claiming a due but resting his whole service on the grace of the God he served.
15:
A new abuse comes under the governor's eye, and the witnesses gather round the profaning of the sabbath. 'In those days saw I in Judah some treading wine-presses on the sabbath, and bringing in sheaves, and lading asses; as also wine, grapes, and figs, and all manner of burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the sabbath day.' The reformed John Gill notes that treading the wine-press was no work of necessity that might drive away the sabbath, but a labour that could well have been deferred to another day. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees in the scene a total disregard of the day. Charles Ellicott marks its spread: in the country Nehemiah observed the most determined profanation, and it reached even to Jerusalem, into which all kinds of burdens were carried on that day as on any other.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a full remonstrance. His own eyes were his informers, Henry says, for magistrates careful to discharge their duty will see with their own eyes and make diligent search to find out the evil; and to his grief there was a general profanation of the sabbath even in Jerusalem, that holy city so lately dedicated to God. The husbandmen trod their presses and brought home their corn, though there was an express command that in earing-time and harvest they should rest, given in Exod. 34:21, precisely because at such seasons men are tempted to think God will indulge them. The carriers loaded their asses with all manner of burdens, though the law had provided for the very cattle to rest in Deut. 5:14, and forbidden burdens on the sabbath in Jer. 17:21.

Henry draws the diagnosis the whole passage rests upon: religion is never in the throne while sabbaths are trodden under foot, and no wonder there was a general decay of religion and corruption of manners among this people when they forsook the sanctuary and profaned the sabbath. The two ruins, the neglected temple of the earlier verses and the profaned day of these, are of a piece. And Henry marks the method Nehemiah will follow — he began by testifying against the offenders, not punishing until he had laid open the evil of it, endeavouring first to convince them that it was a great sin and showing them the testimony of the word against it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the needlessness of the toil, Clarke and Ellicott its brazen extent from field to city, and Henry both the catalogue of the broken laws and the temperate zeal that meets it. Together they set the sabbath in its place as the pulse of a nation's religion, whose profaning is at once the symptom and the seed of every other decay.
16:
Foreign traders had a hand in the profanation, and the witnesses debate what exactly they were doing in the city. 'There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem.' The reformed John Gill takes them to have dwelt there, bringing fish from Tyre and Sidon and the parts adjacent, up from Joppa to Jerusalem, keeping houses or lodgings near the fish gate where they sold. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dispute the sense of the word. Most render it 'dwelt,' they allow, but it is improbable that Tyrians settled at Jerusalem at that time; the verb here means rather to sit, to stay a while undisturbed, to tarry — a trading presence, not a colony. Charles Ellicott holds the middle ground: the men of Tyre had once brought timber for the building of the temple and received food in payment, as at Ezra 3:7, and now they seem to have established themselves as a colony, supplying fish especially to the inhabitants.

So the schools divide over the standing of these Tyrians — whether resident settlers with houses by the fish gate, as Gill and Ellicott suppose, or mere sojourners tarrying to sell, as Keil and Delitzsch prefer. But over the offence they are wholly of one mind. Their fault, Ellicott says, was not their trade but the doing of it 'on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem,' and the verse closes emphatically on that aggravation. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley seizes the same emphasis: it was done in Jerusalem, the holy city, where God's house was and where the great judicatories of the nation sat, and this is added to mark the sin as committed with manifest contempt of both God and man.

The witnesses set the Tyrians beside the Jewish sabbath-breakers of the previous verse to complete the picture. On one side the men of Judah trod their presses and loaded their asses; on the other, heathen dealers spread their fish and wares, and — worse than either — the children of Judah and Jerusalem had so little grace as to buy of them, encouraging the strangers to make the Lord's day a day of merchandise. The guilt, that is, was shared: the foreigner who sold and the covenant people who bought were partners in the same profanation, carried on openly in the holy city under the eye of its rulers. The witnesses do not resolve every question of the Tyrians' residence, but they leave no doubt of the scandal — that traffic forbidden to Israel was being plied by outsiders and welcomed by insiders, in the very place where contempt of the sabbath was most inexcusable.
17:
Nehemiah carries the matter, as before, to the men most responsible, and the witnesses note both the target and the terms of his charge. 'Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said unto them, What evil thing is this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day?' The reformed John Gill takes the nobles to be the rulers of the city, the civil magistrates, whom Nehemiah sharply reproved for their neglect of duty. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the confrontation as a proof laid before them: these evils took place through their negligence, and this Nehemiah demonstrated to their faces. John Wesley explains why the charge fell on the nobles though others did the buying and selling — because, even if the great men did not themselves carry corn or sell fish, the thing was done by their countenance or connivance, and probably by their example, since if the nobles allowed themselves idle recreation on the sabbath, men of business would the more freely profane it with their labour.

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the weight of history behind the rebuke. Keil and Delitzsch have Nehemiah remind the nobles how their forefathers, by such very acts, had brought upon the people and the city great evil — the misery of the former exile and their present oppression — the same sin against which Jeremiah had cried; and he adds that they were now only increasing the wrath of God already lying upon Israel. Charles Ellicott presses the point that the appeal supposes the nobles' familiarity with the express prediction of Jeremiah and its literal fulfilment, the threat of Jeremiah 17:27 that fire should be kindled in the gates of Jerusalem if the sabbath were not hallowed. The rebuke, that is, was no bare command but an argument from their own chronicles.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the boldness and the justice of it. The greatest of men are not too high to be told of their faults by those whose office it is to reprove them; nay, great men should be contended with first, because of the influence they have on others. He charges the nobles with the sin, though they did not personally sell the wares, because they connived at those who did and did not use their power to restrain them, and so made themselves guilty as magistrates who bear the sword in vain — for we must answer for the sins that others are led to commit by our example. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley fix the nobles' responsibility by office and by example, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the appeal to a history and a prophecy they could not deny, and Henry the duty of reproving the great without respect of persons. Together they show a reformer who traced the fault upward to those with power to mend it, and named it, to their faces, 'this evil thing.'
18:
The reproof rises to its sharpest edge in a question drawn from Israel's own calamities, and the witnesses feel its force. 'Did not your fathers thus, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us, and upon this city? yet ye bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath.' The reformed John Gill reads the opening simply — did not your fathers profane the sabbath in like manner? — and lets the parallel between their sin and their fathers' carry the warning. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill out the argument: the fathers by such acts had drawn down 'all this evil,' the exile and the present servitude, and the men now living were only adding to the wrath of God already resting upon the nation; the profanation was not a fresh and untried experiment but the very course that had once ruined them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets out the logic of the appeal in full. Nehemiah reasons the case, he says, showing them that sabbath-breaking was one of the sins for which God had brought his judgments upon them, and that if they did not take warning but returned to the same sins, they had reason to expect further judgments. It is the very reasoning Ezra had used, Henry observes, when he asked, 'If we again break thy commandments, wilt not thou be angry with us till thou hast consumed us?' in Ezra 9:14. The past stroke was not an accident of history but a moral verdict, and to repeat the offence after such a lesson was to invite the sentence over again, and heavier.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse becomes for them a study in the mercy hidden inside a threat. Nehemiah does not merely forbid; he explains, tracing the connection between the desecrated day and the desolated city, so that the nobles might see that in guarding the sabbath they guarded themselves. The words 'ye bring more wrath upon Israel' make the offenders' guilt corporate and cumulative: they were not sinning in a vacuum but piling fresh provocation upon a people not yet clear of the last, endangering the whole community by the greed of a few. Gill fixes the likeness to the fathers' sin, Keil and Delitzsch the identity of that sin with the cause of the exile, and Henry the prophetic certainty that unrepeated warning brings repeated judgment. Together they leave the reader with the sober principle the chapter keeps pressing — that God's past dealings are meant to instruct, that a nation which forgets why it was once punished is preparing to be punished again, and that the profaning of holy time is no small thing but a road the fathers had already travelled to ruin.
19:
From argument Nehemiah passes to enforcement, and the witnesses watch him bar the very gates against the traffic. 'When the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath, I commanded that the gates should be shut, and charged that they should not be opened till after the sabbath.' The reformed John Gill lingers over the phrase 'began to be dark,' or, as it may be rendered, 'were shaded' — when, as Jarchi explains, the shadows of the sabbath's eve stretched out over the gates; for though the sabbath itself began only at sunset and the appearing of the stars, the declining sun cast the shadows of the houses and the surrounding mountains across the entrances beforehand, and at that dusk Nehemiah acted. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes it concrete: after sunset on the Friday evening he caused the gates to be shut and kept them shut all the sabbath; and because he could not trust the ordinary officers, he set some of his own servants to watch, that no one might enter to traffic.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the standing of those servants. They are several times mentioned as employed in public duty, and here they are used provisionally, to keep out the traffickers until the formal appointment of the Levitical guard in the verses that follow, after which they would be relieved. John Wesley reads the same choice as a mark of Nehemiah's prudence: he set his own men at the gates out of a diffidence in those to whom the keeping of the gates was ordinarily committed, trusting the reform to hands he knew.

The witnesses do not divide, and the puritan tradition marks the wisdom of the whole measure. As Matthew Henry read it, Nehemiah aimed at reformation rather than punishment — if he could reform the people he would not punish them — and so he shut the gates from the evening before to the morning after, that no burden should be brought in on the sabbath, nor late the night before, nor early the morning after, lest the holy time be encroached upon at its edges. Those who came to worship in the courts were freely admitted to pass and repass; only those who came to sell were kept out. Gill fixes the exact hour of dusk when the order fell, Clarke the shutting and the trusted watch, Ellicott the provisional nature of the guard, and Wesley the diffidence that prompted it. Together they show a governor who, having testified and reasoned, now made evasion impossible — closing the city itself against the profanation his words had failed to stop, and stationing men he could rely on to hold it closed.
20:
The shut gates did not at once defeat the traders, and the witnesses observe their stubborn expedient. 'So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.' The reformed John Gill pictures the Tyrians and their like camping outside the walls one sabbath or two, unable to get in through such strict watch, and hoping that the Jews would come out to them to buy, since they might not bring their goods within the city. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same manoeuvre and its consequence: because egress from the city could not be refused to the inhabitants, the rest of the sabbath was being broken outside the gates instead of inside them, the traffic merely pushed beyond the wall; and therefore Nehemiah moved to put an end to this evasion also.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the meaning of that 'once or twice.' For a time the merchants lodged outside; but the unseemliness of it, and the plain evidence it gave that they were only waiting to evade the law, made Nehemiah testify in word and threaten forcible action. The very persistence of the traders — returning a second sabbath to try the same trick — exposed their intent, and turned what might have looked like an innocent delay into a settled attempt to keep the profanation alive by the back door.

The witnesses do not divide, and the puritan reading, following Matthew Henry, feels the pathos and the peril of the scene. There the dealers lay encamped before the walls, no doubt wishing the sabbath were gone that they might sell their corn, their whole treasure of the day being how soon the holy hours would pass. It is a picture of the world pressing hard against the fence of a commandment, kept out but not gone, ready to slip in the moment the guard should slacken. Gill fixes their hope that buyers would come out to them, Keil and Delitzsch the leak in the reform that the inhabitants' freedom to leave created, and Ellicott the exposure of the traders' real design by their very return. Together they set up the crisis the next verse resolves: the merchants had found the one gap the shut gates left, and Nehemiah, seeing that a locked city was not enough while custom could be carried on beneath its walls, would have to close even that. The reform, half-won, is shown pressing on to completeness, refusing to leave the sabbath profaned by so much as a market held outside the gate.
21:
Nehemiah meets the traders' persistence with a plain threat, and the witnesses record how effectually it worked. 'Then I testified against them, and said unto them, Why lodge ye about the wall? if ye do so again, I will lay hands on you. From that time forth came they no more on the sabbath.' The reformed John Gill hears in the testifying a solemn protest against their continuance there, a calling of heaven and earth to witness what he would do to them if they did not depart. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the warning: Nehemiah bade the merchants pass the night before the walls no more, threatening, 'If you do this again, I will lay hands on you' — that is, drive you away by force; and from that time forth they came no more on the sabbath, the abuse ended at a word.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the threat more sharply still: 'I will lay hands on you' means 'I will imprison every man of you'; and this, he notes, had the desired effect — they came no more. Whether the menace was of forcible expulsion or of arrest, the witnesses agree that it was credible, because the man who uttered it had already shown he would shut a city and post his own guard to hold it shut; the traders knew he meant it.

The witnesses do not divide, and the puritan tradition draws out the encouragement. As Matthew Henry read the episode, if reformers will but put on resolution, more may be done toward the breaking of bad customs than they can imagine. Vice connived at is a daring thing and will bid defiance to counsel and reproof; but it may be made cowardly, and will be so when magistrates make themselves a terror to it — the king that sits on the throne of judgment scatters away all evil with his eyes. Here was the proof: a settled traffic that had resisted testimony and shut gates alike collapsed the moment it was threatened with a strong hand. Gill fixes the solemnity of the protest, Keil and Delitzsch the meaning of laying on hands, and Clarke the sharper edge of imprisonment; all three mark the swift result — 'from that time forth came they no more.' Together they show that the reform of the sabbath, begun in reasoning and pressed through barred gates, was sealed at last by a governor willing to be feared, and that a firmness which the offenders could not doubt accomplished in a stroke what persuasion alone had not.
22:
The reform is crowned by a settled provision and closed with a prayer, and the witnesses weigh both. 'I commanded the Levites that they should cleanse themselves, and that they should come and keep the gates, to sanctify the sabbath day.' The reformed John Gill takes the cleansing to be from all ceremonial uncleanness, that the Levites might be fit in that sense to discharge their office on the sabbath. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains the double propriety of it: they were to cleanse themselves because the work, though common in its nature, was holy in its design, having respect to the sabbath, and because the day on which they did it was itself the sabbath, for whose observance they were bound to purify themselves; and the gates they were to keep were the gates of the city, entrusted now to the Levites, to whom the sanctifying of the sabbath properly belonged, rather than to the common porters. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confess the brevity of the notice leaves the exact arrangement in some doubt, and weigh the pointing of the words, but take the substance to be that the Levites, purified, were set as the standing guard of the sabbath in the room of Nehemiah's temporary servants. Charles Ellicott adds that the cleansing was required as for a sacred duty, not without reference to their past neglect, which needed to be forgiven — a high tribute to the sabbath ordinance.

Then comes the petition: 'Remember me, O my God, concerning this also, and spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy.' Ellicott hears in it a peculiar pathos of humility, Nehemiah committing his fidelity to the merciful estimate of God. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the added word 'spare me' into a defence of the man. Some have branded Nehemiah as one who dealt with God on the principle of merit; but the very clause proves the contrary, for he expected nothing from God but through the greatness of his mercy. Shame, Clarke says, on those who, with this before them, call so good a man a mere self-righteous worker.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the two petitions the balance of all true devotion. 'Remember me' is the prayer of the dying thief, and that is enough, for God's thoughts toward us are very precious, as in Ps. 40:5; and 'spare me' shows how far he was from thinking he had merited a reward, crying rather, like Jeremiah, to be dealt with gently. The best saints, even in their best actions, stand in need of sparing mercy, for there is not a just man that does good and sins not; and the plea is 'according to the greatness of thy mercy,' not any merit of our own. The witnesses do not divide, and they leave Nehemiah, at the height of his reforming zeal, on his knees, asking not wages but pardon.
23:
The last of the reforms confronts the sin that Ezra's generation had fought before — the marrying of foreign wives — and the witnesses set the scene with grief. 'In those days also saw I Jews that had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab.' The reformed John Gill observes that Ashdod, or Azotus, was one of the five cities of the Philistines, and though the Philistines were not among the seven nations with whom marriage was expressly forbidden, it was very unfit to match with them; the place was a mart of the Arabians, to which the Jews resorted and were thereby ensnared, while unions with Ammon and Moab were flatly unlawful. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read 'saw' as 'visited,' and gather from the fact that these people's children could not speak the Jews' language that they dwelt not in Jerusalem but on the borders of the nations from which their wives came, where Nehemiah found them perhaps on a journey through the province. Charles Ellicott judges from the punishment that followed that these were exceptional cases, but of the most flagrant kind, striking against the law read at the chapter's opening.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees in it the return of a cast-out evil. This very sin had been complained of and much reformed in Ezra's day, in Ezra 9 and following; but when the unclean spirit is cast out, if a watchful eye be not kept, he re-enters, and so he did here. Though in Ezra's time those who had married strange wives were forced to put them away, with all the trouble that caused in families, others would not take the warning — for, Henry says, we still lean toward what is forbidden. And he points to the prophet's rebuke of this very treachery: Judah had dealt treacherously and profaned the holiness of the Lord by marrying the daughter of a strange god, as Malachi charged in Mal. 2:11.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Nehemiah, like a good governor, inquired into the very families under his charge, that he might heal the streams by healing the spring; and that what he found was a breach of the covenant lately sworn, an alliance with the daughters of Ashdod and Ammon and Moab that reached, as the next verses show, into the speech of the children and the house of the high priest itself. Gill fixes the places and their snare, Keil and Delitzsch the border settlements where the intermarried lived, Ellicott the flagrancy of the exceptional cases, and Henry the melancholy relapse into a sin so lately purged. Together they open the final struggle of the book — that a people scarcely cleansed had begun again to mingle the holy seed with the heathen.
24:
The proof of the corruption was on the children's tongues, and the witnesses divide over exactly what the verse describes. 'Their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod, and could not speak in the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people.' The reformed John Gill offers two readings: either the children learned a mixed tongue from their mothers, partly Jewish and partly Philistine; or 'half' refers not to their speech but to their number, that many of them — as Jarchi glosses it — those most with their mothers and chiefly brought up by them, spoke the language of Ashdod. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take it plainly, that half of the children spoke Ashdodite and could not speak the Jews' language, but only the tongue of this or that people from which their mothers were descended.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses a distinct and careful construction. There were, he argues, children in the same family by Jewish and by Philistine mothers; the Hebrew mother would speak to her children in Hebrew or Chaldee, and the Ashdod mother in her own tongue, so that in one household were children who could not understand one another — half, or one part, speaking one language, and the other part another. Since the children of different wives did not ordinarily mingle, and the wives had separate apartments, this, Clarke insists, is a better explanation than the notion that the same child spoke a jargon, half Ashdod and half Hebrew. Charles Ellicott, by contrast, takes the phrase to mean just such a mixture — a blend of Philistine and Aramaic in the children's ordinary speech. So the debate is real: whether 'half' marks two sets of children in a polygamous house speaking two whole languages, as Clarke holds, or a single mongrel dialect on every child's lips, as Ellicott and one strand of Gill suppose.

Beneath the philology the witnesses agree on the alarm the detail sounded. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lessons the tongues taught: children in their childhood learn much of their mothers and are prone to imitate them; if either side be bad, the corrupt nature will incline the child to take after it, which is a strong reason why Christians should not be unequally yoked; and in the education of children great care should be taken about the government of their tongues, that they learn not the language of Ashdod — no impious or impure talk, no corrupt communication. The witnesses do not resolve the grammar, but they resolve the meaning: a generation was rising that could not speak the language of the covenant, and the loss of the mother tongue was the visible token of a deeper loss, the fading of Israel's very identity in the children of these forbidden marriages.
25:
Nehemiah's dealing with the offenders was the fiercest act of the chapter, and the witnesses weigh each stroke of it. 'I contended with them, and cursed them, and smote certain of them, and plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God.' The reformed John Gill takes the contending to be argument, faithful admonition, and sharp reproof. Over the word 'cursed' the schools spread. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as excommunication — he caused them to be cast out of the society of God's people — while Adam Clarke takes it as a denouncing of the judgments of God and the sentence of the law upon them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it as neither a private malediction nor a mere scolding, but the echo of the covenant sanction the people had themselves invoked on this very point in Nehemiah 10:29-30; Nehemiah did but hold them to the curse they had sworn against themselves.

The bodily penalties the witnesses read as measured, not passionate. Clarke understands the smiting as a lawful whipping and the plucking of the hair as a mark of the greatest ignominy, the offenders shaven in disgrace. Wesley agrees that certain of them, whose faults were most aggravated, were beaten with stripes according to the law of Deut. 25:2, and that the hair was shaved because among the eastern nations it was an ensign of liberty, its loss a token of slavery and sorrow. Ellicott sets the gesture against Ezra's: on a like occasion Ezra had humbled himself by plucking off the hair of his own head in Ezra 9:3, whereas Nehemiah plucked the hair of the guilty.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes that contrast the key to the whole scene. It shows, he says, the different tempers of wise and good and useful men, and the divers graces, as well as divers gifts, of the same Spirit: Ezra, in the like case, plucked off his own hair in holy sorrow for the sin; Nehemiah plucked off theirs in holy indignation at the sinners. Neither temper was wrong, and God's work was well done by both. And Henry marks the end to which all the severity tended — Nehemiah made them swear by God that they would not give their daughters to the sons of the heathen nor take the heathen's daughters for their own, binding them by oath against the relapse. The witnesses do not finally divide over the acts, only over the shade of the word 'cursed'; they agree that the punishment was legal, deliberate, and aimed at reformation, and that the passion in it was the passion of a patriot who could not bear to see the holy seed defiled.
26:
To justify so hard a course, Nehemiah reaches for the greatest of examples, and the witnesses dwell on the warning in it. 'Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel; nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin.' The reformed John Gill states the case plainly: Solomon sinned by these very things, marrying strange wives who drew him into idolatry, as the record of his fall in 1 Kings 11 declares. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the argument's turns — Solomon was without peer among the kings of the nations, beloved of his God, set by God over all Israel — and yet, for all that eminence, the outlandish women caused even him to sin; so that Nehemiah asks, by implication, if the wisest and most favoured of kings could not marry heathen wives and keep his integrity, who among these offenders should presume he could?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks a further significance in the appeal. It is implied here, he says, that the language of Scripture concerning Solomon was familiar both to Nehemiah and to the transgressors he rebuked — a remarkable instance of the faithful application of their own chronicles, the reformer arguing not from his own authority but from a history his hearers knew and revered. The example was chosen precisely because it could not be gainsaid.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the full force of the precedent. The falls of great and good men are recorded, he says, that we may take warning by them and shun the temptations they were overcome by. Solomon was famous for wisdom, and there was no king like him for it; yet when he married strange wives his wisdom could not secure him from their snares, but departed from him, and he did very foolishly. He was beloved of God, but this threw him out of God's favour; he was king over all Israel, but this occasioned the loss of ten of his twelve tribes. You plead, Henry has Nehemiah reason, that you can marry strange wives and yet keep the purity of Israelites; but Solomon himself could not — even him did outlandish women cause to sin. Therefore let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall, when he runs upon so plain a precipice. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the sin and its fruit, Keil and Delitzsch the ascending honours that made the fall so terrible, Ellicott the shrewd appeal to a shared and sacred history, and Henry the pointed application to every man's presumption. Together they turn the greatest name in Israel's memory into the strongest argument against the sin now to be purged.
27:
The rebuke gathers into a flat refusal to condone what the law and the example alike condemned. 'Shall we then hearken unto you to do all this great evil, to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives?' The reformed John Gill glosses the sense of it — shall we suffer it to be done, connive at it, and not punish for it? — reading the question as Nehemiah's declaration that authority could not simply look away. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the argument the question carries, tying it back to Solomon: if God spared not Solomon, who was so much beloved of him, shall we spare you, who by your conduct are bringing down God's judgments upon Israel? The lesser cannot claim the immunity denied to the greater.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the refusal in the frame of the whole confrontation. Nehemiah did not seek an occasion against these men, Henry says, but this was an iniquity to be punished by the judge, one he could by no means connive at. 'Shall we hearken to you,' he has the governor answer those who would palliate and excuse the sin, 'you who endeavour to smooth it over? No; it is an evil, a great evil, a transgression against our God, and we must do our utmost to put a stop to it. You beg that your wives may not be divorced from you, but we cannot hearken to you, for there is no other remedy to clear us from the guilt and prevent the infection.' The plea of the offenders — that they might keep the wives they had taken — is met not with cruelty but with the plain necessity of the case.

The witnesses do not divide, and they let the verse show what real reform costs. Henry roots the charge in the precept itself, the command not to give sons and daughters in marriage to the heathen laid down in Deut. 7:3, to which Nehemiah made the offenders swear; for when we would reclaim people from sin, we must show them its sinfulness in the glass of the commandment. Gill fixes the impossibility of conniving, Clarke the argument from Solomon that leaves the transgressors no shelter, and Henry the firm compassion that would not indulge a plea when the whole community's purity was at stake. Together they present a governor who heard the offenders out and still said no — who understood that to hearken here would be to share the guilt, and who counted the pain of the remedy the lesser evil beside the infection it alone could stay. The great evil could not be reasoned into a small one, and Nehemiah would not pretend it could.
28:
The corruption had climbed to the very summit of the priesthood, and the witnesses record how Nehemiah dealt with it there. 'One of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite: therefore I chased him from me.' The reformed John Gill identifies the man as a grandson of the high priest — Eliashib being, on the common reckoning, the high priest here named — and reports that Josephus took him to be Manasseh, the brother of Jaddua the high priest. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees on the identity: this was Manasseh, brother of Jaddua, son of Joiada, and grandson of Eliashib; and 'I chased him from me' means that Nehemiah struck him off the list of the priests and deemed him utterly unworthy of all intercourse with religious people. Charles Ellicott sets the marriage in its scandalous context — Eliashib himself was allied to Tobiah, and now one of his grandsons was married to the daughter of Sanballat, the arch-enemy of the work — so that Nehemiah drove him into exile.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the reason left unstated. The son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, that inveterate foe of Nehemiah and of the whole Jewish community, would not comply with the governor's demand that he dismiss this wife; and therefore Nehemiah was obliged to chase him away, that he might not be a burden or a snare. The offence was aggravated beyond the common marriages, for it joined the house of the high priest by blood to the very man who had laboured hardest to destroy the city.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the long consequence, following Josephus. This expelled priest was that Manasseh who, by Sanballat's interest, procured leave to build the rival Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim; and to him betook themselves the priests who had married strange wives or were otherwise criminal, and, with them or after them, others of the people in like case. Matthew Henry, reading the episode the same way, sees in it the origin of the Samaritan schism that endured to the Lord's own day, when the woman at the well could say, 'Our fathers worshipped in this mountain,' in John 4:20. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the man and his expulsion, Ellicott the doubly scandalous alliance, Keil and Delitzsch the refusal that forced Nehemiah's hand, and Wesley and Henry the schism it bred. Together they show a reformer who spared not even the high priest's own grandson, and whose one act of discipline at the top became, in the providence of God, the seed of a division that outlasted the age.
29:
The expulsion of the priest draws from Nehemiah a prayer against the offenders, and the witnesses weigh what he asks. 'Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood, and the covenant of the priesthood, and of the Levites.' The reformed John Gill reads it straightforwardly as an imprecation — remember them, that is, to punish them, because by marrying strange wives they had defiled the priesthood and rendered themselves unfit to officiate in it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that God will remember their iniquities against them and punish them for their transgressions, but adds that the words are to be understood declaratively: Nehemiah does not so much wish the judgment as announce it, pronouncing what such defilement must draw down.

The grammatical-historical witnesses set the prayer in its larger frame. Keil and Delitzsch treat it as the turn toward the concluding summary of all Nehemiah had effected, the defilement of the priesthood being the last and gravest of the abuses he redressed. Charles Ellicott observes that this priestly violation of the law is committed to God alone for punishment — Nehemiah had done what a governor could do in chasing the man away, and left the deeper reckoning to God — and he explains 'the covenant of the priesthood, and of the Levites': God had chosen the tribe of Levi for himself, and every priest was to be holy to the Lord, as required in Leviticus 21:6; this was the covenant profaned, though there may be an undertone of reference to the great covenant the people had sworn.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a gentler possibility in the same words. 'Remember them, O my God' may be a prayer for their conviction and conversion — Lord, put them in mind of what they should be and do, that they may come to themselves — or it may be a prayer that God would remember the sin against them; and if the latter, it is a kind of prophecy that God would indeed remember it, for those who defile the priesthood despise God and shall be lightly esteemed. Perhaps, Henry adds, the offenders were too many and too great for Nehemiah himself to deal with, and so he refers the matter upward: 'Lord, take the work into thy own hands.' The witnesses do not sharply divide, but they leave a real breadth in the petition — Gill and Clarke pressing the punitive sense, Ellicott the surrender of judgment to God, and Henry alone opening the door to a converting mercy. Together they show a reformer who, having reached the limit of his own authority, commits the defilers of the sanctuary to the God whose covenant they had broken.
30:
Nehemiah gathers his labours into a brief summary, and the witnesses read it as the reformer's own account of what he had wrought. 'Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business.' The reformed John Gill takes the cleansing to reach both people and priests, purged from the strange wives by being made to put them away or else to flee the country; the whole community was purified of the foreign element that had crept in. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the concluding recapitulation of the book: 'I cleansed them from all strangers,' the word for strange denoting the foreign, heathen customs and above all the marriages with heathen women; 'and appointed the wards,' that is, set the posts of service for the priests and Levites, arranging the attendance on the several offices they had to perform at their stations in the temple according to the law.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that this is a brief recapitulation of the special work of Nehemiah after his return, and adds a plausible detail: after the acts of discipline just described, there was doubtless some formal service of expiation, a public cleansing to seal the reform. The verse, that is, does not narrate a new episode but sums up the fruit of all the foregoing — the temple purged of Tobiah, the tithes restored, the sabbath hallowed, and now the people cleansed of their foreign marriages and the ministers set again in ordered courses.

The witnesses do not divide, and they let the sentence carry the double burden it was meant to bear. The negative work and the positive stand together: Nehemiah both cleansed away what defiled and appointed what should endure, removing the strangers and establishing the services, so that the house of God should not again be left forsaken nor its worship fall into confusion. The puritan-evangelical reading, following Matthew Henry, sees in the pairing the whole aim of his government — not the enriching of himself but the purifying of his countrymen as a peculiar people to God, and the setting of every priest and Levite in his own business, that religion might stand on a settled foundation when the reformer himself was gone. Gill fixes the purging of the marriages, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the ordering of the courses and the expiation that crowned it. Together they show a work made permanent by organization, the cleansing sealed and the ministry arranged, as the book draws toward its close.
31:
The book ends where a reformer's heart would end it — with provision for the worship and a plea for mercy — and the witnesses close their account with him. 'And for the wood offering, at times appointed, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.' The reformed John Gill notes that Levites were appointed to receive the wood brought at the fixed times and by the appointed persons, to lay it up in its place and carry it to the altar when needed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls this a most necessary regulation, without which the temple service could not have gone forward, one of the most important of all Nehemiah's provisions, ordered as in Nehemiah 10:34; and he reads the closing prayer, 'Remember me, O my God, for good,' as having precisely the sense of 'O my God, have mercy upon me,' and no other — the cry of a man leaning wholly on grace.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the solemnity of the last sentence. With these words Nehemiah leaves the scene, committing himself and his discharge of duty to the Righteous Judge; his rigorous reformation had brought him into collision not only with external enemies but with many of his own brethren, and it has been assailed by moralists in every age, yet he commits it all to God, as it were by anticipation. And Ellicott adds the wider note that with these words end the annals of Old Testament history — the last sentence of the last of the historical books.

The witnesses do not divide, and Clarke turns the close into a tribute. Nehemiah, he says, might have lived on in ease and affluence at the Persian court, lacking no good thing; but he could enjoy nothing while his people were distressed, the sepulchres of his fathers trodden down, and the worship of his God corrupted. He sought the peace of Jerusalem and was willing to sacrifice wealth, ease, and safety, and even life itself, to restore the desolations of Israel; and for disinterestedness, patriotism, courage, and zeal he stands among the greatest men of his nation. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the last prayer everyone's: 'for good' may well be the summary of all our petitions, for we need no more to make us happy than this. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that the best services done to the public have sometimes been forgotten by those for whom they were done, as the poor wise man was forgotten in Eccl. 9:15; therefore Nehemiah refers it to God to recompense him, and takes him for his paymaster. Together they leave the great governor as he leaves himself — not claiming a wage, but resting his whole life's work on the remembrance of God.
